statement: A stick 12 cm long is cut into three pieces, each a whole number of centimetres long. The three pieces are then used as the sides of a triangle. How many different triangles can be made this way? Triangles with the same three side lengths count as the same.

choices.misconception: I counted every way to cut the stick into three whole-number pieces and did not check which ones can make a triangle.
I also accepted pieces where the two shorter ones add up exactly to the longest, like 3, 3 and 6, but those lie flat and make no triangle.
I counted the same three lengths in a different order as a different triangle.
I forgot that all three pieces can be the same length, 4, 4 and 4.

hints: Can any three lengths make a triangle?
Use the triangle inequality: the two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side. With a total of 12, that means the longest side must be less than half of 12.
The longest piece must be shorter than 6 cm, so it is 4 or 5 cm. List the other two pieces for each case.

solutions.reliable: For a triangle, the two shorter sides must add up to more than the longest. Since all three add up to 12, the longest side must be less than 6 cm, and it must be at least 4 cm because three pieces of at most 3 cm reach only 9. With longest side 4 the only choice is 4, 4, 4. With longest side 5 the other two add to 7 and neither is more than 5, giving 5, 5, 2 and 5, 4, 3. That makes 3 triangles. The transferable idea: turn the triangle inequality into a bound on the longest side, then list systematically from there.

whyOnTest: This checks that you test the triangle inequality strictly, since pieces whose short sides exactly reach the long side cannot form a triangle.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
